overview: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian Renaissance painter and engineer who worked in Florence and Milan and spent his last years in France. He painted the **Mona Lisa** and **The Last Supper**, and filled notebooks with studies of subjects as different as the valves of the heart and the flight of birds.

keyMoments.title: An angel in The Baptism of Christ
keyMoments.text: Leonardo trained in the Florence workshop of **Andrea del Verrocchio**. Both artists worked on The Baptism of Christ, a panel with two angels kneeling by the river. The Uffizi identifies one angel as Leonardo’s and suggests that he also painted parts of the river landscape.

keyMoments.title: The Last Supper in Milan
keyMoments.text: For **Ludovico Sforza**, Leonardo painted the wall of a dining hall at Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan. The painted room seems to extend the real one. Working on dry plaster gave Leonardo time to revise the scene, but the same technique contributed to early paint loss.

keyMoments.title: The Mona Lisa takes shape
keyMoments.text: The Louvre cites an October 1503 note as evidence that Leonardo had already begun the portrait of **Lisa Gherardini**, the wife of a Florentine silk merchant. He painted her turning toward the viewer and used glazes to soften the edges of her features. He kept the portrait for years, continuing to work on it.

keyMoments.title: A new patron in France
keyMoments.text: At the invitation of **Francis I**, Leonardo moved to France in 1516. He settled at the Clos Lucé in Amboise and served the king as a painter, architect and engineer. Leonardo studied the region’s waterways and envisioned a royal palace and drew up plans for a town at Romorantin.

deepFacts.text: While surveying strongholds for Cesare Borgia in 1502, Leonardo drew **a map of Imola** that set the town’s streets inside a circle. Around the rim he wrote the names of winds at the eight points of the compass.

Leonardo studied the hearts of oxen. In his notes, he linked the closing of the aortic valve to eddies in the blood. The Royal Collection identifies a sketch in those notes as a design for a mould for a **glass model** of a heart valve. The collection describes him using the model. A 2002 study cited laboratory flow images as evidence that he may have built it, leaving the question open.

Leonardo’s **Codex on the Flight of Birds** puts notes on birds and flying machines into his right-to-left mirror script. The codex was assembled from partly used sheets, some of them already marked with reddish sketches of plants.
